title: The TCP/IP Stack
description: Explore the four-layer TCP/IP model that powers the modern internet.

data.text: While the OSI model is useful for teaching, the internet actually runs on the TCP/IP model. Named after its two most important protocols — Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol — this four-layer stack is simpler, faster, and built for real-world routing across millions of networks.

TCP/IP was designed in the 1970s by the U.S. Department of Defense. Its goal was to create a network that could survive partial outages, such as a nuclear attack destroying some nodes. That resilience is still baked into the protocol today.

data.title: TCP/IP Layers
items: Application: Protocols like HTTP, DNS, and SMTP that applications use directly.
Transport: TCP for reliable, ordered delivery or UDP for fast, connectionless delivery.
Internet: IP addressing and routing across networks.
Link: Local delivery over Ethernet, Wi-Fi, or fiber.

data.text: TCP and UDP sit at the same layer but make opposite trade-offs. TCP guarantees that every byte arrives exactly once and in the correct order. It does this through sequence numbers, acknowledgments, and retransmissions. The downside is latency and overhead.

UDP skips guarantees entirely. It sends packets without waiting for confirmation. That makes it faster and lighter, but packets can be lost, duplicated, or arrive out of order. UDP is ideal for live video, gaming, and voice calls where speed matters more than perfection.

cards.title: TCP
pros: Guarantees data arrives intact and in order
Handles congestion and retransmits lost packets
cons: Higher latency due to handshakes and acknowledgments

cards.title: UDP
cons: No guarantee of delivery or ordering
Applications must handle loss and duplication

data.text: TCP uses a three-way handshake to start every connection. First, the client sends a SYN packet. The server replies with SYN-ACK. The client finishes with ACK. Only after this exchange can real data flow. This handshake ensures both sides agree on initial sequence numbers and are ready to communicate.

data.caption: TCP three-way handshake establishing a reliable connection.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: SYN (synchronize)
    S->>C: SYN-ACK (acknowledge)
    C->>S: ACK (connection established)
    Note over C,S: Data transfer begins

data.title: Head-of-Line Blocking
data.text: In HTTP/1.1, each TCP connection carries one request at a time. If the first request is slow, every subsequent request waits behind it. This is called head-of-line blocking and is one reason newer protocols like HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 exist.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: TCP/IP is a four-layer model that underlies the modern internet.
TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery at the cost of latency.
UDP provides speed without reliability, suited for real-time applications.
Understanding these trade-offs is essential for choosing the right protocol.
data.takeaway: TCP/IP is not just theory — it is the actual plumbing of the internet, and knowing when to use TCP versus UDP separates senior engineers from beginners.
